units.translation: Fr. 382: "For these groans are the props of their toils." Thus it is read in the scholium on Sophocles' Electra 283, but the reading is suspect, since ἔρεισμα [a prop] can mean nothing other than a support or stay, while here a word is required that has the meaning of relief. Therefore ἰάματα [remedies] is to be preferred, which is read in the Townley scholium on Homer, Iliad 23, 10: unless κουφίσματα [alleviations] should be written with Nauck, since κουφίσματα [alleviations] and ἰάματα [remedies] have been interchanged in a fragment of Menander's Comedies, vol. 4, p. 240.

[with this accent constantly in M, for which everywhere ἐρῆμος should be written. For that the ancient Attics pronounced it thus (and likewise ἑτοῖμος and ὁμοῖος) is established by the testimonies of Herodian and other grammarians. Herodian, On Monosyllabic Words, p. 33, 1: ἐρῆμος: no word ending in -μος of more than two syllables with the circumflex on the penult has η in the penult, but only ἐρῆμος. (Homer, Il. 10, 520) "when he saw the deserted place." The Attics, however, accent the word on the antepenult, where after μέντοι the words οἱ νεώτεροι seem to have fallen out, as the next precept of Herodian about ἑτοῖμος teaches: "and this too among the later Attics they say is accented on the antepenult." And so Eustathius, p. 531, 40: "Herodian says that the word ἐρῆμον and ἑτοῖμον in Homer the later Attics say analogously as ἔρημον and ἕτοιμον." From which the excerpts of Arcadius, p. 61, 6, which are somewhat inaccurate, are to be corrected.] deserted
and they say that Xerxes, alone and deserted, came without many men
